title: Paediatric circumcision
subtitle: Check the anatomy, protect the glans, bipolar only

sources.org: European Association of Urology (EAU) and European Society for Paediatric Urology (ESPU)
sources.title: EAU Guidelines on Paediatric Urology: phimosis

sources.org: American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) Task Force on Circumcision
sources.title: Male circumcision (Technical Report), Pediatrics 2012
Non-therapeutic male circumcision (NTMC) of children: practical guidance for doctors
Holcomb and Ashcraft's Pediatric Surgery: disorders of the penis and foreskin

indications: Pathological phimosis, most commonly balanitis xerotica obliterans (lichen sclerosus) with a scarred, non-retractile foreskin.
Recurrent balanoposthitis, or symptomatic phimosis that has not responded to topical steroid treatment.
Selected boys with recurrent urinary tract infection and an abnormal urinary tract, as a specialist decision.
Non-therapeutic circumcision for religious or cultural reasons, only where lawful and in line with national professional guidance, with consent from those with parental responsibility.
contraindications: Physiological phimosis in a young boy: a non-retractile but healthy foreskin is normal and is not an indication.
Hypospadias, epispadias, chordee, buried or webbed penis, or megaprepuce: the foreskin may be needed for reconstruction, so refer to a paediatric urologist instead.
Known or suspected bleeding disorder until assessed and a haematology plan is in place.
Acute balanoposthitis: treat the infection first.
preparation: Examine the penis yourself: meatal position, ventral shaft, penile size and whether the foreskin is normal.
Ask about family history of bleeding and any personal bleeding history.

Consent for: bleeding, infection, swelling, meatal stenosis (particularly with lichen sclerosus), cosmetic dissatisfaction (too much or too little skin removed, skin bridges, asymmetry), injury to the glans or urethra, altered sensation, and re-operation.
For lichen sclerosus, explain that histology will be sent and that follow-up of the meatus is needed.
positioning: Supine, legs slightly apart, on a warmed mattress for an infant.
equipment: Fine paediatric set, fine artery forceps, curved fine scissors, blunt probe for adhesiolysis.
Bipolar diathermy only; monopolar diathermy is not used on the penis.
anatomy: The prepuce has an outer skin layer and an inner mucosal layer that meet at the preputial ring; in young boys the inner layer is physiologically adherent to the glans.
The frenulum on the ventral side carries the frenular artery, the commonest source of post-operative bleeding, and lies directly over the urethra.
The corona marks the base of the glans; the outer skin incision is made at this level with the skin in its natural position, not under traction.
In lichen sclerosus the scarring may extend to the meatus, causing meatal stenosis.
criticalSafety: Stop if the anatomy is abnormal: a hooded prepuce or a ventral defect means hypospadias until proven otherwise.
Bipolar diathermy only. Monopolar current concentrated in the penile shaft can cause catastrophic tissue necrosis.
Never cut across a clamp without confirming the glans is free of it.
Local anaesthetic for a penile block must not contain adrenaline.
structuresAtRisk: Dorsal neurovascular bundle of the penis
commonErrors: Removing too much shaft skin by cutting with the skin under traction.
Removing too little inner layer, leaving a redundant collar or a residual phimotic ring.
Deep frenular sutures that enter the urethra, causing a fistula.
Relying on the dressing to control bleeding that should have been controlled with bipolar.
complications: Bleeding, usually from the frenular artery, sometimes needing return to theatre.
Meatal stenosis, more common with lichen sclerosus.
Skin bridges, concealed penis or poor cosmetic result.
Urethral fistula or glans injury, rare but serious.
postop: Day-case discharge with weight-based simple analgesia; petroleum jelly to the glans and wound to prevent sticking to the nappy or underwear.
Daily bathing from the next day; swelling and yellow fibrinous exudate on the glans for a week or two are expected.
Return urgently for bleeding that does not stop with firm pressure for 10 minutes, inability to pass urine, or spreading redness.
Follow-up of the meatus where lichen sclerosus is confirmed.

steps.emphasis: Confirm the indication, that the consent is from a person with parental responsibility, and for non-therapeutic circumcision that the legal and professional requirements are met.
Confirm the bleeding history was asked and any haematology plan is in place.
Antibiotics are not routinely needed; follow local policy.
Aqueous antiseptic on genital skin per local policy; let it dry before any diathermy.
Dorsal penile or ring block, or a caudal, with plain local anaesthetic only: never with adrenaline.
Bipolar diathermy only, on precisely identified vessels. Check the frenular area last and with the penis in its natural position.
Place fine absorbable interrupted sutures at 12, 6, 3 and 9 o'clock to align outer skin to inner mucosa, then fill between, without tension or overlap.
Send the foreskin for histology when lichen sclerosus is suspected, and otherwise per local policy.
Record the meatal appearance and any meatal procedure.

step.circ.anatomy-check.title: Anatomy check: stop if circumcision is wrong for this penis
step.circ.anatomy-check.why: The foreskin is the tissue a hypospadias or buried penis repair depends on. Once removed it cannot be replaced, so an unrecognised anomaly turns a simple operation into a lifelong problem.
how: Before any incision, look at the meatal position, the ventral prepuce and the shaft with the child asleep.
A hooded prepuce with a deficient ventral foreskin, a ventral meatus, chordee, a buried or webbed penis, or a megaprepuce means stop.
If an anomaly is found, do not circumcise: close any incision, inform the consultant and the parents, and refer to paediatric urology.
If the meatus is stenosed by lichen sclerosus, plan a meatal procedure within the consent or document it for follow-up.
pitfalls: Assuming the clinic examination was complete.
Proceeding with a partial circumcision on a hooded prepuce.

step.circ.adhesiolysis.title: Freeing the inner prepuce from the glans
step.circ.adhesiolysis.why: The inner prepuce is adherent to the glans in young boys. Until it is separated, the glans cannot be seen or protected, and the meatus cannot be assessed.
how: Gently dilate the preputial opening with fine artery forceps.
Retract the foreskin and separate the inner layer from the glans with a blunt probe, sweeping circumferentially down to the coronal sulcus.
Clean away smegma and inspect the whole glans and the meatus.
pitfalls: Forcing a scarred lichen sclerosus ring and tearing it; a dorsal slit first is safer.
Incomplete separation, so glans tissue is drawn into the excision.

step.circ.marking.title: Marking the outer and inner incisions
step.circ.marking.why: Most cosmetic complaints and concealed penis follow excessive or uneven skin removal. Marking with the foreskin in its natural position, not under traction, sets the amount removed.
how: With the foreskin lying in its natural position over the glans, mark the outer skin circumferentially at the level of the corona.
Retract the foreskin and mark the inner layer a short distance proximal to the coronal sulcus, leaving a narrow cuff, following the V of the frenulum ventrally.
Check the marks for symmetry from all sides before cutting.
pitfalls: Marking with the skin stretched forward, which removes too much shaft skin.
Ignoring the frenular V, producing a ventral skin deficit.

step.circ.excision.title: Excising the prepuce with the glans protected
step.circ.excision.why: Glans injury and amputation are the catastrophic complications of circumcision, and they happen when the glans is not seen at the moment of cutting.
how: Incise the outer and inner marks superficially, through skin only, and excise the sleeve of prepuce between them with fine scissors, staying superficial to Buck fascia.
If using a dorsal slit, place the scissor blade under the foreskin only after the glans is freed and the tip is seen to be in the preputial space.
If any clamp or guide is used, confirm visually and by palpation that the glans lies entirely outside it before cutting.
Control bleeding vessels with bipolar as they are encountered.
pitfalls: Cutting across a clamp without seeing the glans.
Deep dissection on the dorsum into the neurovascular bundle.

step.circ.frenulum.title: Securing the frenular artery
step.circ.frenulum.why: The frenular artery is the usual source of bleeding after circumcision, and it lies over the urethra. Secure control here prevents a return to theatre; too deep a stitch causes a fistula.
how: Identify the frenular artery in the ventral V and coagulate it precisely with bipolar, or ligate it with a fine absorbable suture.
Place the ventral approximating suture superficially, taking skin and mucosa only.
Check the area again after the other sutures are placed, with the penis in its natural position.
pitfalls: A deep figure-of-eight suture that catches the urethra.
Coagulating the frenulum broadly instead of the vessel.
